title: SharePoint Server retirement: what to migrate beyond the files
description: Build a replacement inventory around records, permissions, workflows, and recovery obligations.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: SharePoint Server Is Out of Support. What You Replace.

intro: A SharePoint Server replacement needs to preserve the work attached to each library: permissions, approvals, important links, versions, and retained records. Start with a workflow inventory. Confirm the exact deployed version's support status separately; it determines timing, while the inventory determines what a replacement must do.

sections.title: Inventory the work people perform
sections.html: Start with libraries and sites, then connect each collection to an actual business activity. Record its owner, audience, sensitivity, retention obligation, active integrations, and weekly usage. Ask users to demonstrate approvals, searches, edits, and downloads instead of relying on feature names in a spreadsheet. Two libraries with similar storage size can have very different migration risks when one is an archive and the other drives daily procurement. Confirm the support status of the exact deployed edition and version through its official lifecycle documentation before setting a retirement deadline.

figure.title: What a library migration has to preserve

items.label: Files and versions
items.detail: Working bytes plus the revisions required for later review.

items.label: Access and ownership
items.detail: Ordinary user rights, restricted branches, and accountable owners.

items.label: Business evidence
items.detail: Approval record linked to the exact submitted revision.

items.label: References
items.detail: Old report links resolve through a retained identifier map.

figure.alt: Four layers of a document library replacement: content, access, evidence, and references.
figure.caption: Matching file counts validates only the first layer.

sections.title: Classify what must survive
sections.html: Separate document bytes from metadata, version history, discussion context, and executable workflows. Decide which elements must remain operational and which can become readable historical evidence. A custom approval process may require a redesigned workflow rather than a direct import. Assign a destination and acceptance criterion to every class of information. For old links, choose redirects, an index, or a documented lookup procedure. Keep the source identifiers in a migration manifest so investigators can connect a new record to its previous location without depending on filenames.

sections.title: A replacement map for one library
sections.html:
A migration worksheet should answer a practical question for each item: where will someone complete this task on Monday morning? For a purchase library, that means more than finding a quotation PDF. The buyer needs the active request; the approver needs the submitted revision; finance needs the issued order; an auditor needs the relationship among all three.

Source dependencyDestination requirementAcceptance evidence
Approval listDecision tied to request and versionRetrieve one approved and one rejected request
Library permissionsBuyer and approver access stays distinctAllowed and denied operations under ordinary accounts
Links in monthly reportsResolvable historical referencesOpen a sampled link from an old report

Give each row an owner and a disposition: rebuild, migrate, archive, or retire. Retire only after the owner confirms that nobody depends on the behavior. Rebuilding an approval process can be sensible, but it is a separate delivery item with its own tests. Do not mark it complete because the files arrived. Estimate effort from these dispositions, then schedule the move by business process rather than equal sized storage batches.

sections.title: Pilot a procurement library
sections.html:
Consider a department with purchase requests, quotations, and approved orders. Move a small complete batch that includes a rejected request, a revised quotation, and an order under retention. Have the requestor, approver, and records owner perform their normal tasks in the proposed destination. Compare access as each person, not as an administrator. Open earlier versions and follow links from exported reports. Record every missing behavior with its business consequence. A visually successful file import is insufficient if an approval can no longer be traced to the version actually approved.

Control the transition window

Define when the source becomes read only, how final changes are copied, and who can authorize reopening it. Communicate one authoritative editing location for every migrated collection. Reconcile the final manifest using counts, selected content hashes, permission samples, and business owner review. Preserve a recoverable source snapshot and its required software context according to the agreed policy. The rollback decision should depend on explicit failures such as missing restricted documents or broken approval evidence. Avoid allowing two writable systems to diverge while staff assume synchronization will happen automatically.

figure.title: A controlled authority transfer

items.label: Source freeze
items.detail: Users finish work; source changes stop at an agreed time.

items.label: Final reconciliation
items.detail: Check changed records, content, permissions, and exceptions.

items.label: Owner readback
items.detail: Buyers and approvers execute their actual tasks.

items.label: Destination activation
items.detail: One announced editing location becomes authoritative.

figure.alt: Source freeze, final reconciliation, owner readback, and destination activation in order.
figure.caption: Keep the source recoverable until the destination passes business checks.

sections.title: Retirement sign-off
sections.html:
• Assign an owner and destination to every active library and custom workflow.
  • Verify restricted access, prior versions, important links, and retained records with ordinary accounts.
  • Resolve outstanding exceptions before announcing the new editing location.
  • Test retrieval from the retained snapshot with documented tools and credentials.
  • Schedule decommissioning only after operational ownership and recovery responsibility transfer.

title: Zero-knowledge document editors: workflow and recovery trade-offs
description: Separate cryptographic assurances from the search, recovery, sharing, and administration work a team needs.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: A Zero-Knowledge Editor Is Not a Document Suite

intro: A zero-knowledge editor can limit who sees document plaintext, but you still need to evaluate search, shared ownership, account departure, export, and recovery. The key procurement question is whether the confidentiality model supports your team's full document lifecycle without undocumented manual custody procedures.

sections.title: Define the confidentiality promise
sections.html: Write down the adversaries and system operators the design should exclude. Then request a precise description of where encryption occurs, where keys live, and which components can receive plaintext. A zero knowledge claim should be evaluated against documented architecture and implementation evidence, including browser delivery and key recovery mechanisms. Distinguish document content from metadata such as titles, participant names, timestamps, and object sizes. These fields can still reveal sensitive relationships. Identify the consequences of a compromised endpoint, because encryption against a storage operator does not automatically protect an already unlocked user device.

figure.title: Content secrecy has several boundaries

items.label: Stored ciphertext
items.detail: Verify what the storage operator can learn or decrypt.

items.label: Key holders
items.detail: List users and recovery authorities who can unlock content.

items.label: Unlocked endpoint
items.detail: A compromised device may see content after authorized decryption.

items.label: Metadata
items.detail: Titles, participants, and timestamps need a separate assessment.

figure.alt: Storage, key holder, endpoint, and metadata boundaries of confidential editing.
figure.caption: The confidentiality claim must name the boundary it protects.

sections.title: The recovery decision comes first
sections.html:
Ask two people to sign off on recovery: the confidentiality owner and the continuity owner. Their priorities may differ. A design where only individual users possess keys can reduce server access while making a lost device or departed employee a serious records problem. A recovery custodian can address that problem, but becomes part of the trust model.

User-only custody
Explain how colleagues retain legitimate access if the author loses every authorized device. If there is no recovery path, record that as a business decision with an owner.
Organizational recovery
Identify who approves recovery, who performs it, what information they can see, and how an exceptional unlock is recorded.
Export for continuity
Specify the format, destination protection, and tool required for future reading. A plaintext export has a different exposure boundary from the live encrypted workspace.

Do this before comparing feature lists. Recovery influences group ownership, retention, and incident support. It can also change a seemingly absolute confidentiality statement into a narrower and more accurate one. The appropriate choice depends on what the organization is willing to entrust to custodians and what loss it can tolerate; there is no universally preferable custody arrangement.

sections.title: Exercise a board paper scenario
sections.html: A board secretary distributes a draft paper to six directors, replaces one director, and must retain the final approved copy. Test how the departing director loses future access, how the replacement receives the right keys, and whether previously downloaded material remains outside revocation control. Next, simulate the secretary losing a device. The recovery process must preserve confidentiality while allowing authorized continuity. Ask the records owner to retrieve the approved version without borrowing the secretary's personal account. These exercises reveal practical custody requirements that a successful encrypted editing demo can leave unresolved.

sections.title: List the surrounding team duties
sections.html:
Build a workflow matrix covering shared ownership, membership changes, version retrieval, search, export, accessibility, administration, and retention. Ask whether each operation is supported in the exact candidate configuration and what information it exposes. Server search over plaintext and a design that withholds plaintext from the server require a deliberate reconciliation, such as local search or a different approved mechanism. Do not assume a confidentiality label establishes a particular solution. Evaluate where the workflow becomes slower or relies on manual steps, and give those steps a named operational owner.

Choose recovery intentionally

Key recovery can improve continuity while changing who can unlock documents. Define whether recovery depends on another user, an organization custodian, a hardware device, or a procedure involving several approvers. Measure the process using a disposable account and document. Record what happens when all authorized key holders leave or lose credentials. Export also needs a policy: encrypted exports preserve one boundary but require compatible future tooling, while plaintext exports need protected destinations. Choose the model that matches the organization's obligations and make its remaining limitations visible during procurement.

figure.title: Choose a recovery model with explicit consequences

items.label: User-only keys
items.detail: Lower central custody; document the effect of losing every key.

items.label: Recovery custodian
items.detail: Continuity improves; custodian authority needs approval and audit.

items.label: Protected export
items.detail: Independent readback requires a format, tool, and secure destination.

figure.alt: Three recovery approaches and the continuity or custody trade-offs associated with them.
figure.caption: Recovery arrangements are part of the security design, not a later convenience.

sections.title: Confidentiality review
sections.html:
• Obtain an architecture description for content, metadata, keys, and recovery.
  • Test membership changes and document retrieval with representative ordinary users.
  • Demonstrate search, export, retention, and administrator continuity on a real workflow.
  • Record which endpoints can see plaintext and how their compromise is handled.
  • Assign ownership to every manual procedure introduced by the design.

title: Wiki or office suite? Choose by the information your team produces
description: Compare evolving knowledge pages and structured office files using actual authoring and publishing tasks.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Self-Hosted Office Suite vs Wiki: Which Shape of Work?

intro: Choose a wiki for work whose usefulness depends on connected explanations, and evaluate an office workspace for files whose usefulness depends on calculations, layout, or external delivery. Test those needs in actual candidates. Many teams need both, with an explicit authoritative location for each information class.

sections.title: Identify the primary output
sections.html:
Collect ten recent pieces of work and ask what makes each one useful. An onboarding explanation depends on navigable sections, links, and discoverability. A financial model depends on formulas, cell relationships, and repeatable results. A client presentation depends on layout and delivery in an agreed format. These needs should become acceptance tasks for candidate systems. Verify actual behavior rather than treating a product category as a capability guarantee. Record how often users must exchange files with outsiders and whether the recipient expects an editable artifact or a stable published view.

Follow the revision lifecycle

Some information improves through frequent small edits by many contributors. Other information passes through drafting, review, approval, and archival states. Determine whether the team needs a current answer, a dated deliverable, or both. A policy page might explain the latest procedure while an approved document preserves the legally relevant version. Establish how readers distinguish these states. Consider who can publish, how mistakes are corrected, and where comments belong. A workspace that makes drafting convenient still needs an explicit method for identifying material that has been approved for use.

figure.title: Compare information shapes rather than brand categories

items.label: Connected explanation
items.detail: Find an answer, navigate related pages, and improve shared guidance.

items.label: Structured artifact
items.detail: Preserve formulas, page layout, or an editable external deliverable.

figure.alt: Connected explanations compared with structured office artifacts.
figure.caption: Use the dominant output to choose the first acceptance task.

sections.title: Three outputs, three tests
sections.html:
OutputQuestion to testEvidence to retain
Service handbookCan a new colleague find and follow the procedure?Search terms, route taken, missing links
Staffing modelDo known inputs produce the expected result?Input fixture, formulas, calculated values
Quarterly deckCan the recipient open and revise the delivered artifact?Exported file and downstream readback

This comparison avoids a common category mistake: judging every workspace by how pleasant it is to type a paragraph. A linked page may be excellent for explanation and unsuitable for a calculation that must be recalculated. A spreadsheet may hold the correct numbers while being an awkward place to explain the policy behind them.

If the test favors complementary tools, specify the handoff. For example, the handbook explains staffing rules and links to the current model; the model owns the calculation; an approved deck records the quarterly decision. Assign someone to update the link when the model is replaced. Check permissions at every handoff, because a well maintained knowledge page can still lead a reader to an inaccessible file. Count that maintenance in the operating plan instead of assuming the tools remain coordinated on their own.

sections.title: Test a service planning team
sections.html: Imagine a service team maintaining troubleshooting instructions, a staffing spreadsheet, and a quarterly review deck. Put the instructions through search and cross linking exercises. Put the spreadsheet through a calculation check using known inputs. Export the review deck and inspect it in the recipient's viewing environment. Have the same staff perform all three tasks, noting duplicate entry and lost context. This scenario may justify complementary systems, but it should also reveal who owns links between them. A hyperlink alone does not guarantee that readers have permission to access the linked material.

figure.title: A service planning information chain

items.label: Handbook
items.detail: Explains staffing rules and links to the authoritative model.

items.label: Staffing model
items.detail: Owns inputs, formulas, and expected calculated results.

items.label: Review deck
items.detail: Presents the approved quarterly decision to its audience.

figure.alt: Handbook links to the staffing model, which supports the review deck.
figure.caption: Each object has a different job; duplicated numbers need an update owner.

sections.title: Prevent competing sources of truth
sections.html:
When both types of workspace are needed, assign authority by information class. The approved staffing model can own numerical assumptions, while the knowledge page explains how to use the model. Avoid copying key figures into several independently editable places without a refresh owner. Define stable references and a review schedule for summaries. If one system is unavailable, specify which tasks can continue and which must wait. Self hosting introduces an operating responsibility for each application, including upgrades, backups, identity integration, and support, so include that duplication in the decision.

Workspace responsibilities

  • Test representative explanations, calculations, and external deliverables.
  • Identify the authoritative location for each information class.
  • Check links using users with different group memberships.
  • Verify approved version retrieval and the process for publishing corrections.
  • Estimate the support and recovery work for the complete chosen setup.

title: How to migrate Confluence without a dedicated connector
description: Prepare a manual knowledge migration with explicit handling for attachments, links, permissions, and unsupported content.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Migrating from Confluence Without a Connector

intro: A connectorless Confluence migration needs a source manifest, supported exports, a source-to-destination identifier map, and a deliberate policy for macros and attachments. Pilot a complete handbook before bulk transfer. The real acceptance test is whether users can navigate and trust the imported information with the right access.

sections.title: Create a source manifest
sections.html: Inventory spaces, pages, attachment counts, owners, and permission exceptions using the source system's supported export or administrative methods. Verify the available export formats for the deployed edition; do not assume every format preserves the same metadata. Record source identifiers and parent relationships independently of display titles. Titles can repeat or change during cleanup. Retain an untouched export with a checksum and export date, then work from a separate transformation copy. This creates a reproducible starting point when a conversion rule accidentally removes a table, caption, or important block of text.

figure.title: Minimum useful page migration record

items.label: Source identifier
items.detail: Stable page ID retained even when a title changes.

items.label: Destination identifier
items.detail: New page ID used to resolve internal references.

items.label: Attachment relationship
items.detail: Files remain paired with the page that explains them.

items.label: Exception status
items.detail: Unsupported macro or dynamic behavior has a named owner.

figure.alt: A page migration record showing identifiers, attachments, and exceptions.
figure.caption: The manifest is the basis for repair and reconciliation.

sections.title: Handle unsupported page elements
sections.html: Classify embedded elements such as dynamic reports, diagrams, custom macros, and included pages. For each type, decide whether to recreate behavior, preserve a readable snapshot, or leave a documented exception. Dynamic content needs particular attention because exported output may reflect only one point in time. Ask the page owner whether readers need the underlying query, its latest result, or historical evidence. Keep attachment names and their source page association together. Converting everything into a folder of files can destroy the relationship that makes screenshots and downloadable templates meaningful.

sections.title: Treat broken links as mapping failures
sections.html:
Keep a mapping record for each source page containing its source identifier, parent identifier, destination identifier, export date, and conversion status. Include the source identifier in exception reports even if it will not appear in the public page. Repeated titles and renamed pages make title-only reconciliation unreliable.

source_id: page-042
parent_id: handbook-01
destination_id: guide-117
status: imported
attachment_count: 3
link_review: pending

These are illustrative manifest fields, not a Confluence API schema. Use the actual source export and destination identifiers available in your environment. After import, review unresolved references by target rather than fixing them one page at a time. A single missing included page can break many referring pages; a mapping correction can address the shared cause.

For a macro that cannot be recreated, ask the owner what readers need from it. A static screenshot can preserve an old report's appearance but cannot substitute for a live incident queue. Label snapshots with their date and purpose. Keep executable or interactive behavior in the exception queue until it has a supported replacement, then verify the replacement through a real reader's task.

sections.title: Pilot an operations handbook
sections.html: Select a handbook containing nested pages, a reused procedure, images, and a restricted incident appendix. Import it into the proposed destination and have an operator find a specific recovery step without assistance. Follow internal links and download the associated scripts or templates. Compare the restricted appendix using both permitted and unpermitted accounts. Check whether code formatting and table columns preserve the intended instructions. Record failures by source identifier so corrections can be replayed across the remaining export. This pilot tests usable navigation and confidentiality together, not simply successful parsing of a document format.

sections.title: Reconcile after the final export
sections.html: Set a source editing freeze or define a final change window, then export the remaining delta through a supported procedure. Rewrite internal references using the source to destination mapping. Keep a searchable exception register for pages that require human rebuilding. Owners should approve important content after transformation, especially operational instructions and policy statements. Announce where new edits belong and retain the source in an agreed readable state for a limited period. Without a clear editing boundary, corrections made in the old space can disappear from the new one after migration appears complete.

figure.title: Finalize the knowledge migration

items.label: Freeze edits
items.detail: Stop or explicitly capture changes in the source space.

items.label: Export final changes
items.detail: Apply the supported export procedure and update the manifest.

items.label: Resolve references
items.detail: Use the identifier map to fix internal targets.

items.label: Owner approval
items.detail: High consequence instructions are reviewed before activation.

figure.alt: Final source freeze, export, reference resolution, and owner approval.
figure.caption: Content transfer and an editing-location decision must happen together.

sections.title: Migration closeout
sections.html:
• Reconcile page and attachment counts against the dated source manifest.
  • Verify critical tables, code samples, images, and restricted appendices.
  • Resolve broken references and record deliberate replacements for dynamic elements.
  • Obtain owner approval for high consequence instructions and policies.
  • Preserve the original export and document how its contents can be retrieved.

title: Nextcloud with Collabora: who owns files, edits, and saves?
description: Compare an integrated file platform and editor with a document workspace through owned operations and failure paths.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Collabora in Nextcloud vs a Document Suite

intro: For a Nextcloud and Collabora deployment, verify who stores the authoritative file, who authorizes the editor session, and how an edit becomes a durable saved version. Those responsibilities depend on the installed integration and versions. Compare a document suite using the same request path and failure tests.

sections.title: Map the ownership chain
sections.html: For a candidate involving Nextcloud and Collabora, obtain documentation for the actual integration and installed versions. Identify the owner of file bytes, folder permissions, editing sessions, version history, and save completion. Do the same for the document suite being considered. Packaging alone does not tell you which service persists a change or authorizes an export. Draw the request path from a user's open action through source retrieval and eventual durable storage. Note authentication mechanisms and network routes because configuration failures often occur where one component trusts or contacts another.

figure.title: Trace the configured edit-to-storage path

items.label: User action
items.detail: An authenticated person requests a document operation.

items.label: Access decision
items.detail: The file authority checks the document and requested rights.

items.label: Editor session
items.detail: The editing component loads content through the integration.

items.label: Durable result
items.detail: Verify where saved bytes and version ownership are recorded.

figure.alt: User action, file access decision, editor session, and durable result.
figure.caption: Confirm each owner from the actual integration documentation and test.

sections.title: Use failures to locate the boundary
sections.html:
Three apparently similar complaints point to different owners. A document that cannot open may involve file authorization, source retrieval, or editor initialization. An edit visible to collaborators but absent from a download points toward the save handoff or publication path. An old revision that cannot be retrieved points toward version ownership or recovery state. Trace the configured integration before assigning the ticket.

ObservationFirst evidence to collect
Editor never becomes usableLaunch decision, source fetch result, initialization result
Visible edit is not durableSave event, storage outcome, current version reference
Prior version is missingVersion record and its referenced stored object

These are diagnostic starting points, not guarantees about either product. Keep a disposable workbook whose expected saved value is known. It lets operators reproduce the symptom without requesting a confidential business file immediately. Agree which team gathers each observation and what safe identifier connects the records. The arrangement becomes supportable when a handoff contains evidence of the failed operation, rather than a screenshot passed between administrators who each see healthy processes.

sections.title: Compare the administrative workload
sections.html: List installation, certificate renewal, upgrades, backup coordination, identity changes, and incident diagnosis for the complete configuration. Determine whether components can be upgraded independently and what version compatibility guidance applies. Ask who receives a ticket when a document opens correctly but saving fails. Record supported logs and correlation identifiers without including credentials. A single commercial contact can simplify escalation, but the technical boundary still needs to be understood. Conversely, multiple components can be manageable when the team has a clear operating model and tested responsibilities for every handoff.

sections.title: Follow a budget workbook
sections.html: Use a test workbook owned by a finance group. Open it as an editor and a viewer, change a value, close the session, and download the authoritative saved file. Check formulas and the expected version history using the candidate's documented behavior. Then revoke the editor's group membership during an active session and observe the outcome. Finally, interrupt the connection between the editing component and file authority. These exercises reveal whether users can distinguish a local visible edit from a durably stored result and whether recovery requires action by one administrator or several.

figure.title: A workbook test crosses several ownership boundaries

items.label: Editor and viewer
items.detail: Different accounts execute allowed and denied operations.

items.label: Saved download
items.detail: Known changed value appears in the authoritative file.

items.label: Membership removal
items.detail: Record active-session and new-open access behavior.

items.label: Interrupted handoff
items.detail: Observe the user error and supported recovery procedure.

figure.alt: Four workbook acceptance checks for rights, saving, revocation, and interruption.
figure.caption: An opening demo covers only one part of the integrated service.

sections.title: Judge collaboration as a workflow
sections.html:
Include comments, review, sharing, discoverability, and external exchange in the comparison. Verify each required function in the chosen versions and licensing arrangement rather than inferring it from the product name. Document where users switch interfaces and how they learn which copy is current. If a workflow depends on additional applications, account for their administration and recovery too. Measure startup and save acknowledgement under realistic network conditions. The useful unit of comparison is a completed business task with observable persisted output, including the behavior when one participating service becomes unavailable.

Integrated-service checks

  • Assign ownership for source retrieval, edit authorization, durable saving, and version recovery.
  • Record compatible component versions and the documented upgrade sequence.
  • Test denied access, interrupted saving, and recovery of the budget workbook.
  • Confirm the support escalation path across all involved services.
  • Measure a complete review and external delivery task with ordinary users.

title: Compare ShimoDocs and ONLYOFFICE with a repeatable document test
description: Evaluate ShimoDocs and ONLYOFFICE candidates without substituting brand claims for demonstrated behavior.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: ShimoDocs vs ONLYOFFICE: Fidelity, Open Core, Controls

intro: Compare ShimoDocs and ONLYOFFICE using the same sanitized file corpus, prescribed edits, exported artifacts, permission tests, and written commercial scope. Record exact editions and versions. This produces a decision your team can repeat without treating a vendor's sample files or general feature claims as proof of fit.

sections.title: Assemble a representative corpus
sections.html: Select documents from real work with sensitive details removed. Include long reports with headers and footnotes, spreadsheets with known formulas and charts, and presentations using the organization's fonts. Record the originating application, expected values, and visual reference for each file. Separate must preserve elements from cosmetic preferences. A vendor supplied sample can be helpful during onboarding, but it does not establish compatibility with your estate. Freeze the corpus and its acceptance rules before testing so a later disagreement can be resolved against a common baseline rather than recollection of a demonstration.

sections.title: Measure editing and roundtrip results
sections.html: Open each file, make a prescribed change, save it, and inspect the result in the downstream environment that recipients actually use. Compare pagination, formulas, charts, tracked review information, and any relevant accessibility structure. Record discrepancies with screenshots and the exact file version. Distinguish an unsupported feature from a rendering difference and from content loss. Repeat the same task in each candidate configuration. If a workaround is proposed, measure its user effort and repeatability instead of treating it as equivalent to direct support without further evaluation.

figure.title: The same roundtrip for every candidate

items.label: Frozen source
items.detail: Sanitized file with known layout and expected values.

items.label: Prescribed edit
items.detail: Reviewer performs the same change in each candidate.

items.label: Saved export
items.detail: Capture the actual artifact and exact software configuration.

items.label: Recipient readback
items.detail: Inspect in the downstream environment used for delivery.

figure.alt: Frozen source, prescribed edit, saved export, and recipient readback.
figure.caption: Compare artifacts after work, not only screenshots at first open.

sections.title: Score defects by business consequence
sections.html:
Use an acceptance matrix rather than one overall fidelity score. A misplaced decorative shape and an incorrect total should not cancel each other out in an average. Define severity before the test and assign the decision owner for exceptions.

FindingBusiness questionDisposition
Formula result differsDoes the agreed input produce the correct value?Block this workflow until resolved
Report pagination changesDoes it alter required presentation or references?Owner review against delivery requirements
Required edit needs a workaroundCan ordinary staff repeat it reliably?Measure effort and document the limitation

These dispositions are example test rules, not observations about either product. Use your own business thresholds. Keep each defect tied to the original file, prescribed edit, and exported result. If a configuration adjustment resolves it, rerun the affected test and record the adjustment. When procurement selects an edition, confirm that it includes the configuration and rights used in the passing pilot. A comparison loses value if the tested package and the purchased package differ.

sections.title: Exercise a contract review scenario
sections.html: A legal reviewer opens a contract containing section numbering, comments, and an approval table. The reviewer changes one clause, another user checks the revision, and the final artifact is exported for a counterparty. Verify the specific review functions required by the team in each candidate. Then repeat as a restricted viewer and attempt relevant exports through documented paths. Bind observations to product version, edition, browser, and configuration. This scenario connects fidelity to operational controls: a document that looks correct but exposes an unauthorized operation still fails its acceptance requirement.

sections.title: Read the licensing boundaries
sections.html: Request current terms covering deployment count, users or concurrency, embedding, support, upgrades, and any redistribution. If source availability or an open core model matters, identify which components and editions the statement applies to and obtain the actual license text. Do not infer rights from a repository being publicly visible. Review required controls against the offered edition, because a feature described online may belong to another package. Keep technical results and commercial conditions linked in the comparison so procurement cannot accidentally price a configuration different from the one that passed testing.

figure.title: Commercial scope must match the passing test

items.label: Tested edition
items.detail: Record version, enabled modules, browser, and configuration.

items.label: Usage rights
items.detail: Verify embedding, users, environments, and redistribution terms.

items.label: Support scope
items.detail: Identify escalation, upgrades, and responsibility for defects.

figure.alt: Tested configuration, usage rights, and support scope in an editor purchase.
figure.caption: Source availability alone does not establish every deployment right.

sections.title: Comparison evidence
sections.html:
• Retain the sanitized corpus and expected results for every critical document.
  • Attach observed defects to exact versions, editions, and configuration details.
  • Verify required permissions and downstream export behavior.
  • Obtain written licensing scope and support responsibilities.
  • Recheck unresolved issues using the proposed production configuration before purchase.

title: ShimoDocs or Nextcloud: compare the work, not the folder screen
description: Compare platform fit through file lifecycle, collaborative tasks, integration ownership, and operating effort.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: ShimoDocs vs Nextcloud: File Platform or Document Suite?

intro: Choose between these candidates by testing the responsibility you need to own: a broad file estate, a collaborative document workflow, or both. Include non-office files, approved versions, external delivery, and the extra components required by the offered configuration. An appealing folder view does not answer those questions.

sections.title: Describe the estate and the work
sections.html:
Inventory file types, storage locations, access methods, and the tasks users perform most frequently. An engineering team may manage drawings, exports, photographs, and office files together. A planning department may spend most of its time reviewing shared reports and spreadsheets. Write acceptance cases for the dominant work, including search, sharing, editing, and final delivery. Verify candidate behavior in the exact offered configuration; product categories are useful starting hypotheses but cannot establish format support, synchronization behavior, collaboration controls, or retention capabilities on their own.

Define the authoritative copy

Identify where a document becomes current and how other representations relate to it. Desktop copies, downloaded attachments, converted views, and live editing states can all appear legitimate to users. Specify whether each is authoritative, disposable, or historical. Evaluate how candidates expose this distinction and what happens when users work offline or replace a whole file. If additional editors or services are part of a proposal, map the save boundary and version ownership. A platform decision is incomplete while administrators cannot explain which bytes are recovered after a disputed update.

figure.title: Two acceptance briefs for two kinds of work

items.label: File estate
items.detail: Find, exchange, protect, and recover a varied project package.

items.label: Document workspace
items.detail: Edit, review, approve, and deliver office artifacts.

figure.alt: File estate tasks compared with collaborative document workspace tasks.
figure.caption: Test both briefs if both are central to the organization.

sections.title: Write two separate acceptance briefs
sections.html:
A file-estate brief asks how different objects are organized, located, exchanged, and recovered. A document-workflow brief asks how a team creates, reviews, approves, and delivers its work. Keep both if both matter; do not assume a passing result in one establishes the other.

File-estate acceptance
Include a drawing, photographs, a specialist binary, and office files. Test search, ownership transfer, permission changes, and a complete handover.
Document-workflow acceptance
Include a collaborative report, a calculation model, and an approved presentation. Test the actual edit, review, save, and delivery path.

For each candidate, list the components and manual steps used to pass. The list may include an integrated editor, an archive, a desktop application, or a support procedure. Verify availability and rights for those dependencies in the offered configuration. Ask ordinary users to carry out the tests and capture where they switch interfaces or become uncertain about the current copy.

Make the final choice against the tasks you cannot compromise. A weaker result on a secondary convenience can be acceptable when its cost is explicit; missing a required file handover or approval record cannot be hidden by a higher total feature count.

sections.title: Try a project handover
sections.html: Create a project package containing a spreadsheet, a report, several photos, and a specialist binary file. Ask the project lead to share it with a replacement colleague, revoke an external contractor, and locate the approved report from last month. Have users perform required edits and export a final package for an archive. This example tests broad file handling alongside document collaboration without assuming either candidate provides every step. Record extra applications, manual exports, and administrative interventions. Those dependencies belong in the comparison because they affect training, support, and the consistency of the handover.

sections.title: Price the complete operating shape
sections.html: Estimate administrator time, storage, backups, upgrades, and support for the full proposed stack. Include identity mapping and the maintenance of any bridges to existing business systems. Consider the cost of inconsistent user pathways: separate tools may require users to understand multiple permission and version models. A consolidated workspace may still need external systems for specialized files or records obligations. Gather evidence through a limited pilot and record both technical effort and user completion time. Use measured operating tasks rather than interface impressions to decide whether the proposed structure is sustainable.

items.label: Required integrations
items.detail: Editors, business systems, archive, and identity dependencies.

items.label: Manual work
items.detail: Exports, repairs, permission requests, and user support.

items.label: Recovery

figure.caption: The unit of cost is the complete supported workflow.

sections.title: Platform fit summary
sections.html:
• List the dominant file types and the five most frequent business tasks.
  • Document authoritative storage and version ownership for every editing path.
  • Test a complete project handover using ordinary accounts.
  • Count required external components and recurring manual procedures.
  • Assign support and recovery ownership to the complete proposed deployment.

title: Bank document collaboration rollout: controls for the first pilot
description: Use bounded pilots, access evidence, and operational ownership to introduce collaborative document workflows in banking.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Rolling Out Document Collaboration Across a Bank

intro: Start a bank document rollout with one bounded workflow, named risk and records owners, verified identity mapping, and a measured recovery test. Expand after ordinary users can complete that workflow with the intended access and approval evidence. Deployment alone does not establish compliance with the bank's applicable requirements.

sections.title: Select a bounded first workflow
sections.html: Choose an activity with a clear business owner, predictable participants, and manageable sensitivity. An internal operating procedure review may be easier to validate than customer credit files involving several existing systems. Document the applicable information classification and local policy requirements with the bank's control owners. Specify whether the workspace stores official records or only working drafts. This boundary determines retention, approval, and integration obligations. Avoid implying that deploying a collaboration tool establishes regulatory compliance; the bank must evaluate its configuration, procedures, and evidence against the requirements that actually apply.

figure.title: Choose a bounded banking workflow

items.label: Procedure review
items.detail: Known participants and a clear approval-to-publication transition.

items.label: Customer case files
items.detail: Assess additional systems, information classes, and duties first.

figure.alt: Bounded procedure review compared with a more complex customer case workflow.
figure.caption: Pick the first workflow by its controllable scope.

sections.title: Connect access to staff roles
sections.html: Map membership to authoritative identity groups and identify who approves exceptions. Branch, department, project, and control functions may need different access scopes. Decide how transfers and departures change existing access and active sessions. Test the candidate's documented behavior for these transitions. Shared service accounts should not erase the identity of individual authors or approvers. Also account for support administrators: privileged troubleshooting may expose documents unless the operating procedure limits access. Record the approved path for support investigations and the evidence retained when a privileged action is performed.

sections.title: Decide what the pilot must prove
sections.html:
A useful pilot charter specifies the business event, participants, information class, authoritative record, and expansion gate. For a procedure update, the event is publication of revised branch instructions. The record is the approved version and its decision evidence, not whichever working copy staff opened most recently.

OwnerPilot decision
Operations business ownerWhich task staff must complete and how approval is recorded
Identity ownerHow branch membership and transfers affect access
Records ownerWhere the approved artifact is kept and how it is retrieved
Service ownerHow failed saves and outages are diagnosed and recovered

Use a branch outside the pilot as a negative access test. Ask its ordinary account to search for and open the draft. Then ask a permitted staff member to retrieve the published instructions without assistance from the author. These two outcomes establish different facts: isolation and usable dissemination. Keep the evidence alongside unresolved exceptions. A pilot should pause when a required result is missing, even if participating users are satisfied with the editor itself.

sections.title: Pilot a procedure update
sections.html:
A regional operations team updates a cash handling procedure. Two branches review the draft, a control officer approves a specific version, and staff receive the final published instructions. Run that sequence with test content and actual role assignments. Verify that a third branch cannot access the draft, that the approver can identify the exact reviewed version, and that a staff member sees the intended final copy. Next, remove a reviewer from the project and restore an earlier version in a separate test. Record user completion time alongside every permission and recovery result.

Prepare service ownership early

Assign responsibility for identity incidents, missing saves, disputed versions, unavailable editors, and retention exceptions. Establish support intake fields that capture document identifier, approximate time, operation, and safe correlation information. Avoid requiring employees to send confidential content through unapproved channels for diagnosis. Test backup and recovery with the pilot's actual data relationships. Training should explain the approved location for drafts and final procedures, including how to report a failed save. A rollout becomes difficult to reverse when branches independently invent naming rules, folder policies, and unofficial export practices.

figure.title: Publish instructions with traceable approval

items.detail: Pilot participants review a restricted working version.

items.label: Control approval
items.detail: Decision identifies the exact version reviewed.

items.label: Staff publication
items.detail: Permitted staff retrieve the announced final artifact.

items.label: Recovery check
items.detail: Another operator retrieves the approved record after a test restore.

sections.title: Bank pilot gates
sections.html:
• Obtain business, identity, records, and operations approval for the pilot boundary.
  • Verify cross branch isolation and staff transfer behavior.
  • Bind approvals to the versions actually reviewed.
  • Demonstrate recovery and confidential incident handling.
  • Expand only after resolving pilot exceptions and assigning ongoing support owners.

title: Legal matter collaboration: drafts, issued versions, and preservation
description: Connect matter membership, review versions, external exchange, and preservation duties in one document workflow.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Matter Files: How Legal Teams Run Document Collaboration

intro: Organize legal collaboration around matter membership and the versions exchanged with others. Separate working drafts from issued artifacts, approve external release, and preserve the scope specified by counsel. Account departure and matter closure need tested retrieval procedures so records do not depend on the original author's account.

sections.title: Establish matter access explicitly
sections.html:
Create a matter identifier and assign a responsible lawyer or matter administrator. Document how membership is approved and whether ethical walls or other internal restrictions apply. Check these requirements with the organization's legal and security owners rather than assuming general department access is appropriate. Map the policy to controls supported by the selected platform and record any gap. Matter access should cover search results, attachments, exports, and support procedures as well as opening the primary document. A restricted folder is insufficient if another interface exposes its titles or copied content.

Separate drafts and issued versions

Define states for working drafts, internal review, approved release, and received material. Keep external packages identifiable by version and release date. Users should know whether a link points to a changing draft or the exact file issued to another party. Review comments and change history may require different handling from the clean delivery artifact. Verify what the chosen format and editor preserve, and inspect the resulting export before transmission. Record who authorizes release because technical edit permission alone should not imply permission to send a privileged or confidential document outside the organization.

figure.title: A matter boundary includes more than its main file

items.label: Matter membership
items.detail: Approved people and applicable internal restrictions.

items.label: Working drafts
items.detail: Editable material and review context within the matter.

items.label: Issued artifacts
items.detail: Exact approved package sent to a named recipient.

items.label: Preserved records
items.detail: Retained versions and related material under the applicable scope.

figure.alt: Membership, drafts, issued artifacts, and preserved records within a legal matter.
figure.caption: Different states can require different access and handling.

sections.title: Keep a negotiation exchange ledger
sections.html:
For each outgoing and incoming contract, record the matter identifier, artifact identifier, version, sender, recipient, exchange date, and relationship to the preceding artifact. The ledger can live in an approved business system; it does not need to be invented inside the editor. Its purpose is to establish which document the counterparty actually received and which returned copy responds to it.

matter: MAT-017
outgoing_artifact: agreement-r04
issued_on: 2026-09-10
returned_artifact: counterparty-r04-markup
comparison_base: agreement-r04

The example fields are illustrative. Use your organization's identifiers and approved storage. Compare the return against the issued revision even if internal drafting has advanced to revision six. Otherwise the reviewer may attribute an internal change to opposing counsel or overlook a counterparty deletion.

Include attachments and clean-versus-marked status in the release check where relevant. Ask the responsible lawyer which review material belongs in the package. Then inspect the actual exported artifact; a draft that appears clean on screen can still have unintended context in the delivery format. Keep custody and preservation decisions distinct from release approval. Being required to retain a version does not imply being allowed to distribute it.

sections.title: Walk through a contract negotiation
sections.html: Two lawyers revise a supply agreement, a business owner reviews commercial terms, and opposing counsel returns a marked copy. Label each outgoing and incoming version with its relationship to the negotiation. Have a reviewer compare the returned copy with the actual issued artifact, not whichever draft happens to be current. Test whether business reviewers can access unrelated matter notes. When an external link is used, verify recipient identity, expiry, and the documented revocation behavior. Keep downloaded copies within the risk assessment, because revoking a link cannot reliably recall content already delivered.

items.detail: Use revision four even if the internal draft has advanced.

figure.caption: An exchange ledger prevents ambiguity about the comparison base.

sections.title: Plan preservation and closure
sections.html: Agree which records, attachments, histories, and communications must be retained when the matter closes. Any legal hold or preservation instruction should override routine deletion according to counsel's documented scope. Distinguish disabling ordinary collaboration from deleting records. Assign an owner for later access requests and export. Test a closed matter retrieval using someone other than its original author. If metadata is stored in another matter management system, preserve a stable mapping and reconcile it during archival transfer. This prevents a future investigator from receiving an unexplained folder of similarly named files.

sections.title: Matter closure duties
sections.html:
• Approve membership and verify restricted search, attachment, and export paths.
  • Identify the reviewed and issued versions in every external exchange.
  • Inspect delivery artifacts for unintended review material.
  • Apply preservation instructions before running ordinary cleanup.
  • Test closed matter retrieval and document responsibility for future requests.

title: Public sector document collaboration: records and publication boundaries
description: Define working drafts, official records, access decisions, and accessible publication in public sector workflows.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Document Collaboration in the Public Sector

intro: Separate staff drafts, approved official records, and public release artifacts. Give each transition an accountable owner, apply the authority's retention and access requirements, and inspect the delivered format for accessibility and unintended disclosures. This makes collaboration compatible with explainable decisions and later retrieval.

sections.title: Identify official record transitions
sections.html: Determine when a working document becomes an official record and who declares that state. A draft briefing, an approved decision, and a public release can require different access and retention treatment. Consult the responsible records authority for the applicable schedule and evidence requirements. Store the relevant identifiers and status changes so a document can be connected to its decision process. Avoid relying on a filename containing Final as the approval record. Document the relationship between the collaboration workspace and any official archive, including who transfers the approved artifact and verifies its receipt.

figure.title: An official record needs an identifiable transition

items.label: Draft identifier
items.detail: Connect the working material to its approval request.

items.label: Approved version
items.detail: Identify the exact content accepted by the responsible authority.

items.label: Decision evidence
items.detail: Retain who approved it and when through the agreed process.

items.label: Archive reference
items.detail: Record the destination and verified receipt of the official artifact.

figure.alt: Draft identity, approved version, decision evidence, and archive reference.
figure.caption: A filename containing Final does not establish approval.

sections.title: Three versions can serve different duties
sections.html:
A committee report can have a staff draft, an approved record, and an accessible publication artifact without those objects being interchangeable. The draft supports review. The approved record preserves the decision. The publication artifact serves its audience and may deliberately exclude restricted appendices.

ObjectAuthorityVerification
Working draftAssigned authors and reviewersAppropriate collaboration and denied outside access
Approved recordAuthorized decision and records processExact version, approval, and retrievable identity
Public artifactPublication authorityApproved contents and accessible delivery format

Keep a stable relationship among these objects. A request for the approved decision should not be answered with today's edited draft simply because both share a title. Similarly, the public copy should not silently expose every earlier version available to internal reviewers.

Decide where publication correction happens. An accessible replacement may fix an error, but the authority may also need to retain the original publication and correction history under its applicable policy. Ask records and publication owners to settle that behavior before launch; a content administrator should not have to infer it during a public correction incident.

sections.title: Plan distinct audience pathways
sections.html:
Separate staff drafting, interagency review, contractor participation, and public publication into defined access pathways. Each has different identity and information exposure assumptions. Test the candidate platform's supported controls rather than treating a publicly accessible link as a complete publishing solution. Search previews, comments, attachments, and earlier versions may reveal material beyond the intended release. Administrators need a documented procedure for correcting a mistaken publication. Include the limit that a removed public link does not erase copies already downloaded or indexed outside the authority's systems.

Test a committee report

A policy team prepares a committee report with a restricted personnel appendix. Reviewers collaborate on the draft, a records officer captures the approved version, and a publication officer releases an accessible copy. Walk through that process using harmless test data. Confirm that the public artifact excludes the appendix and internal comments while preserving meaningful headings, tables, and reading order. Test the released file using the authority's accessibility procedure. Then ask a second records officer to locate the approved version and its authorization without assistance from the author.

sections.title: Prepare disclosure and continuity
sections.html: Define how authorized staff search and collect records for a disclosure or information request, with appropriate review before release. A full export may include private drafts and personal information, so collection and disclosure should be separate steps. For service outages, identify essential drafting and publication activities and the approved temporary alternatives. Test recovery of both document bytes and approval metadata. Maintain support procedures that collect safe identifiers instead of encouraging staff to email sensitive reports to technicians. Operational accountability includes who can restore service and who can approve a recovered record for use.

figure.title: Collection and disclosure are separate decisions

items.label: Authorized collection
items.detail: Gather potentially relevant records under the approved request.

items.label: Disclosure review
items.detail: Assess personal information, restrictions, and permitted release.

items.label: Controlled delivery
items.detail: Issue the approved package with its required record of disclosure.

figure.alt: Authorized record collection followed by disclosure review and controlled delivery.
figure.caption: A complete export is not automatically a publishable response.

sections.title: Publication readiness
sections.html:
• Assign record status, publication authority, and retention ownership.
  • Verify staff, partner, and public access using separate test identities.
  • Inspect the released artifact for restricted appendices and review context.
  • Complete accessibility checks on the actual delivery format.
  • Demonstrate retrieval of approved records and recovery of their metadata.

title: A 30-day document platform rollout with measurable gates
description: Organize a thirty day rollout around a bounded pilot, working evidence, support readiness, and expansion criteria.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: A 30-Day Plan for Rolling Out a Document Platform

intro: Use the first thirty days to prove one recurring document task and its support model. Establish a baseline, run real work with a bounded team, test membership and recovery changes, and make an explicit expansion decision. The calendar sets pace; completed tasks and resolved blockers determine readiness.

sections.title: Week one: define the pilot
sections.html: Select one team and a recurring task such as a weekly planning report. Name a business owner, technical owner, support contact, and records contact where needed. Gather a small document set, current completion times, common errors, and access requirements. Confirm identity setup and the supported deployment configuration. Write acceptance criteria that staff can observe: locating the right report, editing with colleagues, retrieving the approved version, and reporting a failed save. Decide where pilot documents are authoritative and how the team will avoid editing competing copies throughout the evaluation period.

figure.title: Four weeks, four concrete decisions

items.label: Week 1: scope
items.detail: Pick a team, task, baseline, authoritative location, and owners.

items.label: Week 2: work
items.detail: Users complete the task and report specific friction.

items.label: Week 3: disruption
items.detail: Test transfers, earlier versions, outages, and support.

items.label: Week 4: gate
items.detail: Expand, revise, or continue against named unresolved criteria.

figure.alt: Four week rollout sequence from scope to work, disruption testing, and expansion decision.
figure.caption: Treat dates as checkpoints, not automatic launch approvals.

sections.title: Week two: perform real work
sections.html: Bring the selected users into the workspace and run their actual task with appropriate test or approved business content. Observe where they hesitate and which actions require help. Training should follow the workflow, including naming, review, final delivery, and error reporting. Keep a short issue log with owner and business impact. Technical setup completion is not an adoption metric. Measure whether staff finish the task and whether its resulting artifact can be located and reused. Resolve permission confusion immediately because early workarounds can become persistent habits across the organization.

sections.title: Measure one report from start to finish
sections.html:
For a weekly planning report, capture a small baseline: preparation time, review handoffs, time to locate the approved copy, and incidents requiring support. Repeat the same observations during the pilot. Keep the participants and report complexity visible so the comparison is not mistaken for a controlled performance study.

Useful adoption evidence
A staff member completes review and finds the correct output without intervention from the implementation team.
Useful support evidence
A designated responder identifies an opening or saving failure using the runbook and safe identifiers.
Weak evidence on its own
Accounts created, invitation messages sent, or browser tabs opened. These indicate activity but do not establish task completion.

Ask users what caused work to leave the approved path. A mailed attachment might indicate missing external access, unclear version labels, or a failed save. Fix the cause and rerun the task instead of reporting the attachment as mere resistance to change.

At the end of the month, select one of three decisions: expand this workflow, revise it and repeat the relevant test, or continue the bounded pilot while a specific blocker is resolved. Name the blocker and owner. That makes an extension actionable rather than an indefinite pilot with no acceptance boundary.

sections.title: Week three: test difficult days
sections.html: For the planning report, remove a participant, add a replacement, restore an earlier version, and simulate an unavailable editing service using safe test conditions. Ask the support contact to diagnose one failure using the runbook. Have the business owner retrieve the approved report without its author. Compare task time and error frequency with the baseline while acknowledging the small sample. These exercises expose dependencies that enthusiastic pilot participants may conceal by helping each other informally. Update support instructions and ownership rules before introducing additional teams with less direct access to the implementation group.

figure.title: A difficult day tests several kinds of readiness

items.label: Participant removal
items.detail: Check both new requests and an already open session.

items.label: Earlier version
items.detail: Another user retrieves the approved report without its author.

items.label: Service interruption
items.detail: Observe the recoverable error and supported return to work.

items.label: Support handoff
items.detail: A designated responder uses evidence available in the runbook.

figure.alt: Membership, version, outage, and support readiness checks for the pilot.
figure.caption: These transitions expose dependencies a happy-path pilot can hide.

sections.title: Week four: decide what expands
sections.html:
Review unresolved issues with their owners and separate launch blockers from tolerable limitations. Choose expansion by workflow and information class rather than assuming every team can reuse the pilot configuration. Confirm capacity, backup responsibility, and support coverage for the next cohort. Communicate the editing location and the transition date for any replaced process. Keep the old path available only according to a defined transition rule. If the pilot has not met essential criteria, extend it with a specific corrective objective instead of announcing a successful organization-wide rollout because the month has ended.

Month-one decision

  • Record baseline and pilot task completion results.
  • Verify access changes, version retrieval, and ordinary user support.
  • Assign owners and deadlines to unresolved limitations.
  • Confirm operating capacity and recovery responsibility for the next cohort.
  • Publish a clear decision to expand, revise, or continue the bounded pilot.

title: Document platform exit planning: test the exported collection
description: Test export, metadata recovery, permission translation, and downstream usability as an ongoing portability obligation.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: Leaving a Document Platform: Lock-In and the Exit Path

intro: An exit plan should prove that people can use exported documents without the original platform. Test current files, required versions, metadata, approvals, and access mappings through a small handover. Confirm extraction rights and timing in writing, then measure the effort needed to reconstruct any missing context.

sections.title: Define the portable collection
sections.html: List the material the organization must retain after departure: current files, selected earlier versions, folder relationships, ownership, comments, approval evidence, and retention status. Assign importance and a proposed destination to each class. Ask for current export documentation and contract terms covering bulk extraction, assistance, fees, and the period after termination. A right to export should identify the available formats and included metadata. Keep the requirements separate from current capability claims until they have been verified. Some information may need an archival representation rather than continued interactive behavior in the destination.

figure.title: What must remain useful after exit

items.label: Content
items.detail: Current artifacts and required historical versions.

items.label: Relationships
items.detail: Source IDs, folders, approval evidence, and linked context.

items.label: Access intent
items.detail: Owners and audience rules translated for the destination.

items.label: Runtime needs
items.detail: Tools and rights required to read any retained formats.

figure.alt: Content, relationships, access intent, and runtime needs in a platform exit.
figure.caption: A folder of downloads may preserve content while losing the other layers.

sections.title: Define a portable acceptance package
sections.html:
Choose a completed project and produce a package that stands on its own. Include a manifest naming source identifiers, versions, exported filenames, formats, and required context. Document which representations are editable and which are preserved only for historical reading.

Package memberIndependent readback
Approved reportRecipient can identify the approved version and its decision
Calculation modelKnown input gives the expected result in the intended tool
Access mappingRecipient can distinguish intended audience from exported custody
Exception registerMissing interactive behavior has an owner and reconstruction plan

Give the package to someone without an account on the source platform. If that person needs to ask the author which file is final, the export still depends on informal knowledge. Fix the manifest or record relationship and repeat that task.

Time the extraction and reconstruction separately. Export may be fast while rebuilding links, review history, or permissions is slow. Use these measured stages to estimate the termination window and assistance needed. Keep the package protected: portability concentrates information and can create broader custody than the live workspace allowed.

sections.title: Distinguish readable and reusable
sections.html: A rendered document can preserve appearance while losing formulas, structured headings, comments, or editable objects. Decide which outputs need to remain reusable and which need only a stable historical view. Test both with the software that future users can actually obtain. Keep checksums and a manifest linking exported files to source identifiers and versions. Filenames alone are weak evidence when several documents share a title. If an export depends on proprietary tooling, document licensing, runtime, and long term availability requirements so the archive does not become unreadable after the original service contract ends.

sections.title: Run a project exit rehearsal
sections.html: Choose one completed project with a spreadsheet, report, presentation, restricted appendix, and approval record. Export it through supported methods, then give the package to a colleague without access to the original workspace. Ask that person to identify the approved report, recompute a known spreadsheet result, and explain who could access the appendix. Attempt an import into the likely replacement or an archival repository. Record what needs reconstruction and how much effort it takes. This scenario turns portability from a vague feature into a measured handover with visible information losses.

items.label: Exit estimate

sections.title: Plan the final extraction window
sections.html: Estimate export duration, rate limits, storage, transformation time, and owner review using the rehearsal results. Agree when users stop editing and how final changes are captured. Include identities that may have been removed and documents under preservation obligations. Secure exported packages as carefully as live data; bulk extraction can concentrate confidential material in one place. Define verification before deleting or surrendering the source. The contract should leave enough time to resolve failed batches and obtain assistance, since discovering an incomplete export after account closure creates a much harder recovery problem.

sections.title: Exit readiness
sections.html:
• Confirm extraction rights, available formats, assistance, and termination timing.
  • Test representative files and metadata outside the original platform.
  • Measure reconstruction effort and assign ownership to known gaps.
  • Protect bulk exports and reconcile them against a source manifest.
  • Repeat the rehearsal after major platform or workflow changes.

title: Self-hosted document platform costs: build the recurring operating budget
description: Estimate infrastructure and staff costs using workload, recovery obligations, support duties, and change frequency.
author: Office SDK Editorial

references.label: ShimoDocs: What a Self-Hosted Document Platform Costs to Run

intro: Budget a self-hosted document platform from its service promise: workload, supported hours, recovery targets, and change frequency. Include administrator time, test and recovery environments, backups, and support alongside infrastructure and licensing. A deployment quote cannot show what it will cost to keep the service dependable.

sections.title: Start with the service promise
sections.html: Define supported hours, availability expectations, response times, recovery targets, and the document population. Identify the planned number of active editors, peak opening rate, typical file sizes, and conversion workload. These assumptions drive the infrastructure estimate and the operating tasks. Separate production, test, recovery, and administrative environments. A low cost production footprint can be misleading when there is no safe place to rehearse upgrades or recover a backup. Make assumptions explicit and identify who can approve a changed service promise if the estimated budget cannot support the original expectations.

figure.title: Recurring cost follows the service promise

items.label: Production resources
items.detail: Compute, database, storage, and network for the tested workload.

items.label: Operational effort
items.detail: Identity, incidents, patching, monitoring, and user support.

items.label: Recovery resources
items.detail: Protected backups, restore environment, and rehearsal effort.

items.label: Planned changes
items.detail: Upgrade tests and integrations included as named budget items.

figure.alt: Production, staff, recovery, and change cost layers for a document service.
figure.caption: An existing employee's time still consumes operating capacity.

sections.title: Count recurring human effort
sections.html: List identity administration, patching, certificate renewal, monitoring review, backup checks, restore rehearsals, incident response, and user support. Estimate effort from observed tasks or a pilot, then attach staff rates or internal capacity costs. Include coordination with storage, database, network, and security teams. A task performed by an existing employee still consumes capacity even if it does not create a new invoice. Record which duties can be automated and the maintenance required for that automation. Avoid assuming the initial installer will silently become the permanent service owner without an agreed allocation of time.

sections.title: Use a cost worksheet with visible units
sections.html:
Give every line a unit and an assumption. Infrastructure may be priced per month; administrator effort per hour; backup storage per retained byte; support coverage by an agreed arrangement. Keep those units visible so a change in retention or staffing can be recalculated without rebuilding the entire estimate.

annual baseline =
  12 × monthly infrastructure
  + 12 × monthly staff hours × hourly cost
  + annual license and support
  + planned change and recovery work

This is a budgeting relationship, not a vendor pricing model. Add only the categories applicable to the actual proposal, and avoid counting support effort twice if a contract already covers a defined task. Costs excluded from the baseline should still appear as separate assumptions.

For example, extending support from business hours to continuous coverage affects staffing even if machine usage stays unchanged. Increasing retained versions affects storage and restore work even if the number of users stays flat. Show a base case and one plausible growth case, with the changed inputs highlighted. Ask the service owner to confirm the promised operating outcome for both. That is more useful than an unexplained contingency percentage because reviewers can see which requirement causes the additional cost.

sections.title: Model a concrete annual budget
sections.html:
Suppose a service uses infrastructure costing an illustrative 1,200 currency units monthly and requires 30 staff hours at 60 units per hour. Its recurring baseline is 3,000 units monthly, or 36,000 annually, before licensing and project changes. Add separately estimated recovery storage, upgrade rehearsals, and support coverage. The example is arithmetic, not a vendor price or sizing recommendation. Replace each assumption with local evidence. Showing staff effort alongside infrastructure reveals why reducing machine cost by a small amount may be less valuable than simplifying an unreliable maintenance procedure.

Expose variable and exceptional costs

Storage growth, retained versions, large imports, network transfers, and expanded support hours can change the baseline. Identify which costs grow with users, bytes, activity, or environment count. Budget major upgrades and integration changes as planned events rather than hiding them in a generic contingency. Consider a recoverable failure scenario: replacement infrastructure, investigation effort, communication, and lost staff productivity all affect the decision. Use sensitivity ranges for uncertain inputs. A budget with visible assumptions is easier to revise than a precise total assembled from untested capacity and workload estimates.

figure.title: Two growth inputs change different costs

items.label: More active editors
